posts:
Meta bans TikTok ads across its apps to stifle rivalry under market pretexts.
Evidence: ByteDance ad ban, platform monopoly weaponized, competitor block.
#Meta #TikTok #TechPolicy 🌐

Meta framed the ad ban on ByteDance as standard business practice, stating they aren't obligated to run ads for a competitor whose goal is pulling users away.
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

Reality reveals a monopolistic platform weaponizing its market dominance to crush a rival while deflecting from massive child safety settlements and regulatory heat.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.75, -0.8) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Meta weaponizes its platform dominance against a rival under the false pretext of routine business competition.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 4)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Meta Platforms: FAIL (-0.75, -0.8) — Weaponizes ad monopoly to stifle rival.
- Business Pretext: FAIL (-0.8, -0.85) — Masks anti-competitive retaliation as routine.
Meta banned TikTok and ByteDance ads across the US, Canada, Japan, and other nations, escalating platform wars shortly after a major $17B child safety settlement.

The Poison:
Masking aggressive anti-competitive market exclusion and monopoly power as mundane business housekeeping avoids necessary antitrust scrutiny.
This is a classic plane error: conflating who holds market power (WHAT/WHO plane) with a neutral contractual dispute. Meta uses platform gatekeeping to punish rivals.

Social Physics Analysis:
Meta runs a Smart Selfish Maneuver: using platform monopoly power to squeeze a competitor, wrapped in the neutral pretext of normal business operations.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map stated business housekeeping against monopolistic retaliation, it plots toward Lesser Evil. Net negative forces drive market division.

The Unavoidable Truth: Platform monopolies control digital access and freely weaponize it against rivals.
The Unavoidable Lie: This ban represents neutral, routine business competition.

Alethekanon:
When corporate giants invoke 'routine business practice' to justify exclusionary retaliation, they conceal raw monopoly enforcement behind administrative jargon.

Awwthekanon:
It's sad to watch multi-billion-dollar tech empires use everyday users and businesses as pawns in their endless playground turf wars instead of building safe spaces.

Brothekanon:
Classic corporate slap fight. Meta gets hit with massive child safety fines, then turns around and bans TikTok ads like it's just normal business. Wild stuff.

Spirithekanon:
"He who loves quarrel loves transgression; he who builds his gate high seeks destruction." Proverbs 17:19 FAIL
Erecting towering gates to crush rivals while feigning peace breeds systemic decay.

Meta has banned ads from TikTok’s Chinese parent company ByteDance across the US and several other countries as the rivalry between the major social media operators heats up, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The ban, which went into effect on Thursday, restricts ads and paid marketing messages from ByteDance, along with third-party ads that link to TikTok.

“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Christopher Sgro said in a statement to The Verge. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”

The move comes just months after Meta agreed to a major child safety settlement, requiring it to pay $17 billion and add new restrictions for teens. Meta has since called on TikTok and YouTube to impose similar safeguards, including by waging an ad campaign that TikTok reportedly declined to share on its platform. TikTok has also stopped allowing users to include links that “open or log you into other social media apps,” according to its support page

Though TikTok in the US is now controlled by a joint venture majority-owned by US-based companies, ByteDance remains a major shareholder. In addition to pulling TikTok ads in the US, the policy will also restrict them in Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam.
